newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lebed launches new party with eye on Kremlin.
newsitem.headline: Lebed launches new party with eye on Kremlin.

text.p: General Alexander Lebed, undeterred by two false starts, launched a third bid for the Russian presidency on Friday with a new political party he said would take power this year.

The popular retired paratroop commander came closest to his Kremlin goal last autumn, when President Boris Yeltsin's heart problems increased the prospects for an early election and Lebed's own rating rose to record highs.
Yeltsin's apparent recovery this month has dimmed those prospects. But Lebed showed no signs of patience as he opened the first congress of his Russian Popular Republican Party.
"We're not here because Lebed took it into his head to create a party. No," Lebed said in his characteristic growl.

"The people asked us to create this party," he added. He said the 10,000 members it had attracted so far represented all sections of Russian society, which he said had been deceived and robbed by the current leadership.
Brushing off suggestions that Yeltsin would serve out the second four-year term he won in last July's election, Lebed said his rival's recent reappearance in public life would be shortlived.
"It's not a return to politics," Lebed told a news conference. "It is Boris Nikolayevich's swansong," he said, making a pun on his own last name, which means "swan" in Russian.
"What we see today...is the death throes of power," he said. "It will simply collapse...like its predecessors collapsed in 1991. It's unavoidable. It will happen this year, 1997."
"We won't actively provoke this but...we have to be ready to grab power as it falls," the 46-year-old general said.
The hall, packed mainly with middle-aged men in brown and grey suits, applauded politely as Lebed said that God was with the party and called on the government to step down.
"If you can't do your jobs then you must go, the sooner the better. It will clean up the atmosphere," he said.
Lebed raised the spectre of civil unrest if the government stayed in office, saying a nationwide strike planned for March 27 could be the catalyst. But he denied he favoured the use of force.
But his hour-long speech lacked some of the punch which marked his bid for the presidency last July, when he came third.

The idea behind the party is to create a grassroots vehicle for Lebed, who is bitterly opposed by the establishment and lacks the powerful financial backers who helped keep Yeltsin in office. Lebed has always denied speculation that the Kremlin funded him last year as a spoiler against the communists.
Asked who financed the congress, which brought several hundred delegates from all parts of the country to an ornate assembly hall in central Moscow, he said it was party members.
"It's a party of the middle class, of small and medium-sized entrepreneurs and they finance their party," he said.
Lebed's first foray into politics involved joining forces with the small Congress of Russian Communities in 1995, but he parted company with it last year after arguing with its leaders.
